text.p: Unemployment in Britain plunged by nearly 96,000 -- the largest fall on record -- to below the psychologically important two million level in November, the Office for National Statistics said Wednesday.

The ONS also published robust retail sales figures for November that provided further evidence of vigorous economic growth, increasing pressure on the Conservative government to raise interest rates before a general election due by next May.
Unemployment fell in November to 95,800 to 1.929 million, adjusted for seasonal variations, the first figure below two million since early 1991.
"What we can see as we come to Christmas 1996 are perhaps the best economic prospects that we have seen across the United Kingdom for a very long time," Prime Minister John Major said.

However, City of London economists said the jobs and high street sales figures would make it harder for the government to resist Bank of England pressure to raise interest rates from the present 6.0 percent to choke off inflationary pressures.

The Conservatives, who lost their overall majority in parliament after a by-election defeat last week, are anxious to avoid raising interest rates again before the election as this would mean more expensive home loans for millions of people.

The opposition Labour party, which is well ahead of the Conservatives in opinion polls, poured scorn on the jobless figures, saying they could only be explained by people being driven off the unemployment register.
"No-one believes their bogus figures. More people believe in Santa Claus," said Labour's deputy leader, John Prescott.

The dramatic drop in unemployment was partly due to the introduction of a new "jobseekers' allowance" and changes in rules for benefits. These two factors accounted for a drop of around 25,000 in the jobless count.
That still left a drop of around 70,000 in the underlying figure, nearly three times what the markets were expecting.

"The fact that this sharp fall in unemployment has not yet resulted in any increase in earnings growth is extremely encouraging," said the Confederation of British Industry, Britain's leading business organisation.
Unit wage costs eased slightly to an annual growth rate of 4.6 percent in the three months to October from 4.7 percent in the three months to September.
